title: Recursion
summary: Base case, smaller subproblem, and an honest stack story.

parts.rule: A recursive function needs a base case that returns without calling itself, a move to a strictly smaller subproblem, and a clear account of what the call stack holds. Tail recursion is a special case some runtimes optimize; most interview languages do not promise that. Depth n on a skewed input uses O(n) stack space.
parts.why: Tree and divide-and-conquer prompts are recursion-shaped. Missing base cases infinite-loop; wrong smaller step never reaches the base; deep left-skewed trees blow the stack. Interviewers also ask you to rewrite recursion as an explicit stack to prove you understand the hidden memory.
parts.example: Factorial of 4: f(4) → 4*f(3) → 4*3*f(2) → 4*3*2*f(1). Base f(1)=1, then unwind 2, 6, 24. Stack frames peak at depth 4. Binary tree sum on root 1 with left 2 and right 3: sum(node)=node.val + sum(left) + sum(right); sum(null)=0. Evaluation visits 2, then null children, returns 2; visits 3, returns 3; returns 1+2+3=6. Bad version without null base never stops. Convert the tree sum to an explicit stack: push root, pop and add values, push children — same O(n) work, stack object instead of call frames. Prefer the explicit form when n can be 10⁵ and default recursion limits are lower.
parts.use: Use recursion for tree and graph DFS, divide-and-conquer, backtracking, and definitions that are naturally inductive. Use an explicit stack when depth may be large or the interviewer asks for iterative form.
parts.refuse: Refuse recursion without a base case. Refuse a recursive step that does not shrink the problem. Refuse ignoring O(depth) stack space on skewed inputs. Refuse mutual recursion that obscures the termination argument in an interview setting.

body:
Rule. A recursive function needs a base case that returns without calling itself, a move to a strictly smaller subproblem, and a clear account of what the call stack holds. Tail recursion is a special case some runtimes optimize; most interview languages do not promise that. Depth n on a skewed input uses O(n) stack space.

Why it matters. Tree and divide-and-conquer prompts are recursion-shaped. Missing base cases infinite-loop; wrong smaller step never reaches the base; deep left-skewed trees blow the stack. Interviewers also ask you to rewrite recursion as an explicit stack to prove you understand the hidden memory.

Worked example. Factorial of 4: f(4) → 4*f(3) → 4*3*f(2) → 4*3*2*f(1). Base f(1)=1, then unwind 2, 6, 24. Stack frames peak at depth 4. Binary tree sum on root 1 with left 2 and right 3: sum(node)=node.val + sum(left) + sum(right); sum(null)=0. Evaluation visits 2, then null children, returns 2; visits 3, returns 3; returns 1+2+3=6. Bad version without null base never stops. Convert the tree sum to an explicit stack: push root, pop and add values, push children — same O(n) work, stack object instead of call frames. Prefer the explicit form when n can be 10⁵ and default recursion limits are lower.

When to use. Use recursion for tree and graph DFS, divide-and-conquer, backtracking, and definitions that are naturally inductive. Use an explicit stack when depth may be large or the interviewer asks for iterative form.

When to refuse. Refuse recursion without a base case. Refuse a recursive step that does not shrink the problem. Refuse ignoring O(depth) stack space on skewed inputs. Refuse mutual recursion that obscures the termination argument in an interview setting.
